content.text: An LLM keeps nothing between API calls. The context window is the text of one request plus the reply being generated: working memory for that call, gone when it ends. Chat "memory" is your app, or the chat product, sending the history again or injecting saved notes, and the model's weights never change because of your conversation.

A developer wires a support chatbot to an LLM API. In the demo, the user types "Hi, I'm Mona", then "What's my name?", and the bot says it doesn't know. The ticket reads: "Model forgets context. Try a bigger model?" A bigger model won't help. The bug is one line: the code sends only the newest message, so the model never saw the first one.
The common misconception
"The model remembers earlier chats and learns from them, because the conversation is stored inside it." Plenty of experience points that way:

items.text: In a chat app, the assistant refers back to something you said twenty messages ago, as if it had been listening all along.
Chat products manage history for you, so you never see that it's being sent again.
Give a model three examples of a format and it follows the pattern. That looks like learning.
Some assistants recall your preferences across separate chats.

content.text: The half-truth: within one request, the model really does use everything in front of it. But "in front of it" is the whole story. Nothing is written back into the model, and nothing carries over to the next request unless someone sends it again.
What actually happens
Every call starts from zero

Anthropic's docs put it directly: the Messages API is stateless, so you always send the full conversational history. Each request carries the system prompt and every earlier turn your app decided to include. The model reads that, generates a reply, and the request is over. Its parameters were fixed when training ended; your conversation doesn't change them.

Even when a provider keeps the conversation for you, the model still isn't remembering. Anthropic's message threads (in beta) let a later request send only the new messages, but it's storage around the model, and a thread expires five minutes after its last request. The history is still fed back in as input.
The context window is working memory for one request
The
context window

is all the text the model can reference while generating a response, including the response itself. Anthropic's docs call it a "working memory", distinct from the huge corpus the model was trained on. Everything counts against it: the system prompt, every message, tool definitions and results, and the output being generated.

In a conversation, each user message and assistant reply accumulates, so every new request is bigger than the last. The window has a hard size, up to 1M tokens depending on the model, and a request whose input alone exceeds it fails with a "prompt is too long" error. Size isn't the only limit: the docs warn that accuracy and recall degrade as the token count grows, which they call context rot.
In-context learning isn't training
The GPT-3 paper showed that a large model can do a new task from a few examples written into the prompt, applied "without any gradient updates or fine-tuning". That's
in-context learning
: the examples steer this request only. Leave them out of the next request and the skill leaves with them. Correcting the model in chat works the same way: the correction is just more context.
So where does "memory" come from?

From code outside the model. Your app stores the messages and resends them; a chat product may drop or summarize the oldest turns to fit; a memory feature saves notes and puts the relevant ones back into the prompt. Anthropic's memory tool makes the split explicit: Claude asks to read or write files under
/memories
, your application performs those operations on storage you control, and the docs say the memory lives entirely in your application.
See it in code
Both versions call the same stateless API with the official Python SDK. The first sends only the newest message; the second keeps the history in the app and sends all of it every time.

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
✅ Right
tabs.code:
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()
history = []  # the conversation lives in your app, not in the model

def ask(text):
    history.append({"role": "user", "content": text})
    reply = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=16000, messages=history
    )
    history.append({"role": "assistant", "content": reply.content})
    return next(b.text for b in reply.content if b.type == "text")

ask("Hi, I'm Mona.")
print(ask("What's my name?"))  # works: both turns are sent again

content.text: The right version appends
reply.content
, the full list of blocks, not just the text, so anything the API needs back on the next turn is preserved. It reads the answer from the first
text
block rather than
content[0]
, because a reply can start with other blocks, such as thinking.

rows.text: Your app or the chat product stores it and sends it again
The context window is long-term memory
It's one request's working memory: input plus the reply being generated
Examples and corrections teach the model
They steer this request only; the weights don't change
A bigger window means it remembers everything
It holds more, but recall degrades as the context grows
Memory features live inside the model
They're storage outside it that puts saved notes back into the prompt

blocks.title: Keep conversation state like any other state

content.text: Store messages in your database keyed by conversation ID, load them for each request and append the reply. It survives restarts, works across servers and gives you an audit trail of exactly what the model saw.

blocks.title: Resent history is paid for every time

content.text: Because every turn resends the whole history, input tokens grow with each message, and so do cost and latency. Long sessions eventually hit the window limit and the request fails. Trim, summarize or compact before that happens, not after a user reports it.
How to apply it in your project
Treat the message list as application data. Persist it, version it and decide in code what each request includes.
Count tokens before sending long requests and set a limit below the model's window. When a conversation nears it, summarize older turns or use the provider's compaction feature.
Store durable facts, such as a user's language or plan, in your own tables or a memory tool. Inject only the relevant ones into the prompt, and let users see and delete them.

items.title: Put lasting corrections in the prompt

content.text: If users keep correcting the same behavior, the model won't learn it from them. Fix it once in the system prompt or in your examples, and verify the change with an evaluation.
Key takeaways

items.text: The model is stateless between calls: it only knows what the current request contains.
The context window is working memory for one request, including the reply, not storage that persists.
In-context learning and in-chat corrections steer one request; they never update the weights.
Chat memory is built outside the model, by storing history or notes and sending them again.
Resending history costs tokens every turn, so budget, trim and compact deliberately.
